findings.text: Per-thread and process CPU timer queues are discarded at thread and thread-group teardown through dedicated exit entry points that walk all three clock bases and detach queued nodes.
Common timer update helper normalizes the repeat interval from the new setting and resets overrun bookkeeping when a timer is programmed.
CPU clock query interface validates the clock, reports tick granularity except for the scheduler clock, rejects attempts to set a CPU clock, and samples current consumption for reads.

Clock to process resolution rejects out-of-range clock kinds, maps an encoded zero identifier to the caller or its thread group, requires thread clocks to stay within the caller thread group, and requires process clocks to identify a live thread-group leader with a special alias for gettime.

Periodic CPU timer advancement leaves disarmed or unexpired timers unchanged and otherwise moves the expiry forward by whole intervals while accumulating a missed-expiry count using a scale-up then scale-down accumulation that avoids multiplication overflow.
Expiry cache is considered inactive only when all three per-clock next-event hints indicate no pending expiry; thread versus process timer storage is selected by the per-thread flag of the clock.
CPU time sampling distinguishes scheduler runtime from user and system accounting, with one clock observing scheduler runtime, one observing user plus system, and one observing user only.

Clock validation, timer creation, timer queries and target lookup execute under read-side RCU protection, while timer deletion, programming and rearming acquire the target sighand lock through a retry loop that tolerates exit and reaping and warns if a vanished target still appears queued.

Per-task and per-signal CPU timer state holds three clock bases each with a timer queue and a next-event hint plus activity flags, and each timer carries queue linkage, an expiry-list link, firing state and ownership of a process identifier.

Timers move among disarmed, armed, firing-list and expired states: arming enqueues and refreshes the earliest-expiry hint, disarming dequeues and requests hint recalculation when the earliest entry was removed, firing disarms and either wakes a sleeper or queues a signal while clearing one-shot expiry, and rearming advances then requeues interval timers.

Periodic expiry checks sample current consumption, drain due timers into a firing list while refreshing next-event hints, handle deadline overrun, interval timers and resource-limit timers, and release tick dependency and activity flags when no expiry remains.

Expiry processing caps the number of timers collected in one pass and defers the remainder by returning the next expiry, while programming or deleting a timer already on the firing list suppresses its signal and requests a retry instead of mutating the list.

Timer programming samples the clock under lock, reports prior remaining time, converts relative deadlines to absolute form, arms only enabled future expiries that require notification, forces hint recalculation when left disarmed, and fires immediately when the new deadline already passed.

Resolution fact: tick-derived granularity for ordinary CPU clocks and one nanosecond for the scheduler clock; collection cap twenty per pass; idle next-event uses maximum unsigned value; disabled interval stored as zero and overrun restart uses negative one.

Resource-limit supervision sends privileged signals at soft and hard thresholds for CPU time and real-time runtime, logs when fatal-signal diagnostics are enabled, advances the soft threshold after each soft notification, and stops further process checks at the hard limit.

Timer creation resolves and holds a reference on the target identifier under RCU, assigns the CPU timer operations, initializes queue linkage and expiry-list linkage, and selects a distinct lock class when expiry runs in task-work context.
